title: Reading DNA by Stopping the Copy
endLine: Stopping copies at known bases turns DNA order into fragment length.

scenes.tts: How do you read the order of bases along a DNA strand? Sanger sequencing turns that challenge into sorting by length. It copies the strand, stopping different copies at every base.
scenes.caption: How do you read the order of bases along a DNA strand? Sanger sequencing turns that challenge into sorting by length. It copies the strand, stopping different copies at every base.
scenes.visual: Schematic workbench world filling most of the frame height (no molecular structures): across the top runs a single-stranded DNA template shown as dark mystery tiles marked '?'; below it, glowing schematic copy bars grow from left to right and halt at staggered lengths, then drift down into a neat staircase sorted shortest to longest as their end tiles light up in four bright base colours.
scenes.narration: How do you read the order of bases along a DNA strand? Sanger sequencing turns that challenge into sorting by length. It copies the strand, stopping different copies at every base.

scenes.visual: Carried workbench world dimmed gently in the background with slow ambient drifting coloured base tiles; bold high-contrast title 'Reading DNA by Stopping the Copy' fades in and holds cleanly for 2 seconds.

scenes.tts: Start with a single-stranded template and a primer, a short DNA strand paired to it. The primer gives the copying enzyme, polymerase, a three prime end, where new nucleotides join. Add ordinary nucleotides plus a little chain-stopping dideoxynucleotide. Each stopper keeps a normal base and five prime triphosphate, so polymerase adds it.
scenes.caption: Start with a single-stranded template and a primer, a short DNA strand paired to it. The primer gives the copying enzyme, polymerase, a 3' end, where new nucleotides join. Add ordinary nucleotides plus a little chain-stopping dideoxynucleotide. Each stopper keeps a normal base and 5' triphosphate, so polymerase adds it.
scenes.visual: Schematic workbench (no molecular structures): the top template track settles in place first; a bright primer bar docks at its left end with a glowing '3'' connector notch; a geometric polymerase block snaps onto the primer; a pool of ordinary coloured base tiles (each with a front '5'' tab and back '3'' notch) drifts in alongside a few starred dideoxynucleotide tiles that have the same '5'' tab and base colour, and polymerase snaps one stopper cleanly onto the growing copy.
scenes.narration: Start with a single-stranded template and a primer, a short DNA strand paired to it. The primer gives the copying enzyme, polymerase, a 3' end, where new nucleotides join. Add ordinary nucleotides plus a little chain-stopping dideoxynucleotide. Each stopper keeps a normal base and 5' triphosphate, so polymerase adds it.

scenes.tts: A dideoxynucleotide stops a copy for good. It lacks the three prime hydroxyl the next nucleotide must bond to. At each site most copies take an ordinary nucleotide, and a few take a stopper. So stops fall at every position. Stopping copies at known bases turns DNA order into a ladder of fragment lengths.
scenes.caption: A dideoxynucleotide stops a copy for good. It lacks the 3' hydroxyl the next nucleotide must bond to. At each site most copies take an ordinary nucleotide, and a few take a stopper. So stops fall at every position. Stopping copies at known bases turns DNA order into a ladder of fragment lengths.
scenes.visual: Schematic close-in on the same copying track (no molecular structures): the starred stopper tile's right edge is flat and capped ('No 3'-OH'), so the next incoming ordinary tile bounces off and the polymerase detaches; zoom slightly back inside the same world as parallel copy bars run across the template, most extending past each site while occasional stoppers halt copies at consecutive single-base lengths, forming a clean schematic ladder of lengths.
scenes.narration: A dideoxynucleotide stops a copy for good. It lacks the 3' hydroxyl the next nucleotide must bond to. At each site most copies take an ordinary nucleotide, and a few take a stopper. So stops fall at every position. Stopping copies at known bases turns DNA order into a ladder of fragment lengths.

scenes.tts: Next, sort the stopped copies by length. Classically, four tubes each held one stopper type, or terminator. Four gel lanes separated pieces differing by one nucleotide. Later, each terminator got its own fluorescent dye, so one reaction holds all four. A capillary sorts fragments by size while a detector reads each colour.
scenes.caption: Next, sort the stopped copies by length. Classically, four tubes each held one stopper type, or terminator. Four gel lanes separated pieces differing by one nucleotide. Later, each terminator got its own fluorescent dye, so one reaction holds all four. A capillary sorts fragments by size while a detector reads each colour.
scenes.visual: Schematic transformation in the lower zone of the same world (no molecular structures): first, four vertical gel lanes ('ddA', 'ddC', 'ddG', 'ddT') pull bands downward by size so single-nucleotide steps form crisp rungs; then the four lanes merge smoothly into one slender glass capillary tube as the four terminators gain four distinct fluorescent dye glows; fragments stream shortest-first past a laser detector beam that plots coloured schematic peaks in sequence.
scenes.narration: Next, sort the stopped copies by length. Classically, four tubes each held one stopper type, or terminator. Four gel lanes separated pieces differing by one nucleotide. Later, each terminator got its own fluorescent dye, so one reaction holds all four. A capillary sorts fragments by size while a detector reads each colour.

scenes.tts: Now a direction puzzle. Suppose a detector reports the shortest fragments in order as A, C, and G. What are the new strand and its template, each written five prime to three prime?
scenes.caption: Now a direction puzzle. Suppose a detector reports the shortest fragments in order as A, C, and G. What are the new strand and its template, each written 5' to 3'?
scenes.visual: Same schematic capillary detector readout in high contrast: three bright coloured peaks appear from shortest to longest and stamp the letters 'A', 'C', 'G' into three slots; below them appear two empty labelled prompts: 'New strand (5'→3'): ?' and 'Template (5'→3'): ?'.
scenes.narration: Now a direction puzzle. Suppose a detector reports the shortest fragments in order as A, C, and G. What are the new strand and its template, each written 5' to 3'?

scenes.visual: Hold the schematic 'A', 'C', 'G' peaks and both question prompts ('New strand (5'→3'): ?' and 'Template (5'→3'): ?') steadily on screen for 4.5 seconds while a subtle glowing progress bar sweeps across the bottom.

scenes.tts: The copy grows from the primer at its three prime end, so the shortest fragment holds the first new base. The new strand reads five prime A, C, G, three prime. Its antiparallel template pairs opposite as three prime T, G, C, five prime. Written five prime to three prime, that is C, G, T. Complementing without reversing reads the template backwards.
scenes.caption: The copy grows from the primer at its 3' end, so the shortest fragment holds the first new base. The new strand reads 5'-ACG-3'. Its antiparallel template pairs opposite as 3'-TGC-5'. Written 5' to 3', that is CGT. Complementing without reversing reads the template backwards.
scenes.visual: Same schematic readout resolves step by step: first a small arrow shows the copy growing away from the primer's '3'' end, with the shortest fragment holding the first new base; '5'-ACG-3'' drops from the peaks into the new-strand bar; directly above it, paired complementary tiles snap in antiparallel as '3'-TGC-5''; then that template bar flips end-for-end horizontally so its '5'' end moves to the left, reading '5'-CGT-3'', while a struck-through warning tag 'Not TGC' flashes briefly to mark the direction check.
scenes.narration: The copy grows from the primer at its 3' end, so the shortest fragment holds the first new base. The new strand reads 5'-ACG-3'. Its antiparallel template pairs opposite as 3'-TGC-5'. Written 5' to 3', that is CGT. Complementing without reversing reads the template backwards.

scenes.tts: Sanger reads are accurate, but limited. Each reaction reads one region, commonly up to about eight hundred to one thousand bases. Because the first few dozen bases are often poor, experimenters cannot rely on the start. And reporting bases is not locating them across repeated genome segments.
scenes.caption: Sanger reads are accurate, but limited. Each reaction reads one region, commonly up to about 800 to 1,000 bases. Because the first few dozen bases are often poor, experimenters cannot rely on the start. And reporting bases is not locating them across repeated genome segments.
scenes.visual: Schematic capillary trace widens along the workbench: clean, sharp peaks span a bracket marked 'Schematic: 800 to 1,000 bases', while the leftmost region turns jagged and is bracketed 'Poor first few dozen bases'; zooming out along a long genome track below, one read bar slides back and forth between two identical repeated blocks marked '?', showing it cannot pin down which repeat it belongs to.
scenes.narration: Sanger reads are accurate, but limited. Each reaction reads one region, commonly up to about 800 to 1,000 bases. Because the first few dozen bases are often poor, experimenters cannot rely on the start. And reporting bases is not locating them across repeated genome segments.

scenes.tts: In nineteen seventy-seven, Sanger, Nicklen and Coulson published chain termination, using DNA from the phage phi X one seventy-four. It became the basis of most DNA sequencing for the next quarter century. In nineteen eighty, Sanger shared half of the Chemistry Nobel with Walter Gilbert, his second Nobel.
scenes.caption: In 1977, Sanger, Nicklen and Coulson published chain termination, using DNA from the phage phiX174. It became the basis of most DNA sequencing for the next quarter century. In 1980, Sanger shared half of the Chemistry Nobel with Walter Gilbert, his second Nobel.
scenes.visual: Carried workbench shifts smoothly into a clean schematic timeline ribbon anchored beneath the glowing capillary trace: marker '1977' lights up with 'Sanger, Nicklen & Coulson' and a schematic circular 'phage phiX174' ring filling with colour-coded read tiles; a small '1980' marker labelled '1980 Chemistry Nobel (shared)' lights next; then a long glowing span runs forward from 1977 labelled 'Basis of most sequencing: next quarter century' (no end year drawn).
scenes.narration: In 1977, Sanger, Nicklen and Coulson published chain termination, using DNA from the phage phiX174. It became the basis of most DNA sequencing for the next quarter century. In 1980, Sanger shared half of the Chemistry Nobel with Walter Gilbert, his second Nobel.

scenes.tts: Fluorescent capillary Sanger chemistry produced most of the sequence in the February two thousand one human genome drafts. The International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium and Celera Genomics each published one. The consortium's finished sequence of two thousand four covered about ninety-nine percent of the gene-rich euchromatin, still with gaps. One missing hydroxyl turned DNA order into readable lengths.
scenes.caption: Fluorescent capillary Sanger chemistry produced most of the sequence in the February 2001 human genome drafts. The International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium and Celera Genomics each published one. The consortium's finished sequence of 2004 covered about 99% of the gene-rich euchromatin, still with gaps. One missing hydroxyl turned DNA order into readable lengths.
scenes.visual: Same schematic timeline extends to 'February 2001' as parallel capillary lanes stream coloured reads into a long schematic chromosome bar labelled '2001 human genome drafts'; two small tags 'Consortium' and 'Celera Genomics' attach to it. Then the bar advances to '2004' filling to 'About 99% euchromatin' with small marked gaps left open (schematic); finally the camera pulls gently back to the single stopped copy bar and its flat end cap.
scenes.narration: Fluorescent capillary Sanger chemistry produced most of the sequence in the February 2001 human genome drafts. The International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium and Celera Genomics each published one. The consortium's finished sequence of 2004 covered about 99% of the gene-rich euchromatin, still with gaps. One missing hydroxyl turned DNA order into readable lengths.

scenes.visual: Clean high-contrast end card over softly drifting coloured base tiles from the carried world, displaying verbatim: 'Stopping copies at known bases turns DNA order into fragment length.' Held for 3.5 seconds.
